judge_panel.reason: The paper's own conclusions state 'Future work will focus on deploying the DCCNN on real-time data acquisition with operating qubit hardware, validating the simulation-trained model on measured scans and demonstrating in-loop integration with the QICK control firmware.' This confirms that real-time, in-loop operation has NOT been demonstrated, yet the abstract calls it 'an online detector' and 'a control-loop primitive' as if already achieved.

The paper presents the method as already achieved in operation (e.g. “an online detector of charge jumps ... is presented” and “This shifts charge-jump detection from a post-hoc diagnostic to a control-loop primitive”), but the evidence is still synthetic/estimated: “the network is trained on synthetic Ramsey tomography scans” and “Vitis HLS C-synthesis ... estimates a per-inference latency,” while “Future work will focus on deploying the DCCNN on real-time data acquisition ... and demonstrating in-loop integration.”

The paper explicitly lists physical in-the-loop implementation as future work, stating, "Future work will focus on deploying the DCCNN on real-time data acquisition with operating qubit hardware... and demonstrating in-loop integration with the QICK control firmware" (Sec. V), which confirms the reviewer's concern that the achievement is overstated.

judge_panel.reason: The paper's conclusions acknowledge 'Future work will focus on...validating the simulation-trained model on measured scans,' confirming no held-out-qubit or real-data validation is provided, yet the abstract claims the model requires 'no per-qubit hyperparameter tuning' as a demonstrated property across all qubit configurations tested only on synthetic data from the same five qubits used in training.

The manuscript makes forward-looking generalization claims such as “A single trained model serves all five qubit templates” and “requires no hyperparameter tuning when applied to a new qubit,” but it shows no held-out-qubit/device or measured-data validation; indeed it states “Future work will focus on ... validating the simulation-trained model on measured scans.”

The conclusions claim that the approach "requires no hyperparameter tuning when applied to a new qubit"; however, as Section II.C notes, the training data was generated from "each of the five qubit configurations," meaning the model was never validated on a held-out, previously unseen qubit.

judge_panel.reason: The paper states 'the χ² algorithm parameters were tuned...to maximize jump-tagging efficiency subject to a false-positive-rate (FPR) constraint of 5%. This FPR was chosen to match the rates observed for the DCCNN before and after quantization (6% and 4%, respectively).' This describes approximate matching to a range rather than exact ROC-curve matching, making it unclear whether the comparison is truly at a matched operating point, but the methodology is at least partially described.

The paper claims comparison at a “matched false-positive rate,” yet Sec. III.C says the χ² method was tuned “subject to a false-positive-rate (FPR) constraint of 5%,” and that “This FPR was chosen to match the rates observed for the DCCNN before and after quantization (6% and 4%, respectively).” That is only an approximate compromise, not a truly matched operating point for the compared quantized DCCNN.

While the abstract claims the comparison is at a "matched false-positive rate," Section III.C states that the χ² FPR constraint was set to 5% "to match the rates observed for the DCCNN before and after quantization (6% and 4%, respectively)." The threshold was not strictly matched to the 4% FPR of the quantized DCCNN.
